The third installment of ALLi's “Spammers and Scammers” series turns away from email scams to tackle a different problem: scraping someone else's book wholesale and reselling it under a fake author name, something that happens mainly on Google Play Books.

blocks.cap: ALLi's scam-watch series on books being sold under fake names.

blocks.x: Reports to ALLi's Watchdog Desk are rising from authors whose books were duplicated and reposted under someone else's name. It is plagiarism on a large scale, and even when ALLi and the affected authors notify Google, a response takes weeks to months. Because these operators post hundreds to thousands of books at once under a single fake pen name, the damage multiplies quickly.

The gap lies in Google Play Books' partner program. Anyone can register as a publisher, and there is still no process to verify whether the registrant actually holds the rights. Even authors who filed takedown requests through the formal process weren't given a processing timeline, and some got no reply at all. ALLi found that the Google Books team only reaches out when there's a problem with a request, meaning silence doesn't necessarily mean inaction.

There is still no complete prevention. Here is what ALLi recommends: set up Google Alerts for your name and book titles, but check manually and regularly too, since alerts aren't perfect. Even if you have no plan to sell there, listing your book in the Google Play Books Partner Center helps when you need to prove authorship. Linking your author profiles across Google Books, your website, and your social accounts is another option. Watermarks won't stop theft, but they can help trace how a copy leaked. ALLi doesn't recommend DRM for this problem, since it mainly inconveniences readers who actually paid for the book.

If it has already happened to you, there is a process. On the copyright removal form at support.google.com/legal, select Google Play or Google Books and file a formal DMCA notice. List each infringing listing's URL individually, and submit your own genuine edition, ISBN, and publication date as evidence. If even one of these is missing, the request gets delayed or ignored. The notice must be sent by you or a properly authorized representative; notices from third parties are generally ignored.

Report the account, not the book. Reporting a single title only gets that single title handled. Reporting the account for impersonation and systematic infringement gives Google grounds to take down the entire listing at once. If there is no response after six weeks, check for missing items and resend, keeping a record of the dates sent and referencing the prior notice in every follow-up.

ALLi asked anyone who has gone through something similar, whether the takedown succeeded or failed, to report it to the Watchdog Desk. The more patterns accumulate, the stronger the case becomes for everyone affected.

A petition calling for a legal requirement that AI companies disclose their training data has topped 10,000 signatures. On the UK Parliament petitions site, 10,000 is the threshold at which the government must respond. Past 100,000, a petition is considered for parliamentary debate.

blocks.cap: Anna Ganley, chief executive of the Society of Authors.

blocks.x: The petition is titled “Protect creators' rights: demand AI companies disclose training data.” Its demand is fairly specific: it asks for enough detail about the works used to train generative AI that creators can check whether their own work was used, assert their rights, negotiate licenses, and receive fair payment.

The petition states that what creators need are rules that guarantee consent, formal licensing, and fair compensation. It does not stand against technological progress; it stands for moving forward within a balanced regulatory framework.

Months of calls from the UK publishing industry for transparency-first regulation have gained a number attached to them for the first time. The deadline is October 29, 2026. How many more signatures come in before then will decide whether this demand ends with a single written response or makes it to the parliamentary debate table.
The article was written by Maia Snow for 「The Bookseller」 on August 13, and ran alongside a photo of Anna Ganley, chief executive of the Society of Authors.
This is not a regular episode. Elizabeth Ann West and Stacey Anderson spent an hour mapping out The Ultimate Automated Author Experience, which Future Fiction Academy will release this fall.

The core idea is a way of working that isn't tied to any one model. Models change, tools disappear, and prices shift. Debate over watermarking and detection keeps moving too. The proposal is to build an author process that holds up no matter what OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or Amazon does next.

There are three standalone courses: Build Your Own AI Writing Studio, for building your own AI writing studio; Your Author Voice Print, which measures your style to capture your voice like a fingerprint; and Professional Manuscript Analysis with AI, for deep manuscript review.

There are five fall intensives: designing a repeatable AI workflow, building a living writing environment, an editing system where humans and AI work together, automating the marketing function, and final packaging through to publication.

West and Anderson are clear on one point: this isn't a curriculum that hands you a single prompt. It teaches you how to build your own studio, understand your style, analyze manuscripts, make workflows repeatable, and run editing, marketing and publishing with safeguards in place.
Later in the video, the two say their goal is for students to no longer need them. Enrollment is limited.
Mega members should not buy it separately — it's already included in the membership. Everyone else can pre-order individual courses, intensives, or the full bundle.
Their definition of the stack is clear: my computer, my files, my knowledge base, my scripts, my AI, my publishing system.

Educational and professional publishers are embracing AI far more deeply than trade publishers. McGraw Hill CEO Philip Moyer put numbers to that gap when he released first-quarter results for the period ended June 30.
Revenue rose 2.6% to $549.9 million. EBITDA climbed to $207 million from $191.4 million in the same period last year.
Moyer said AI has played a part in revenue growth, margin improvement, price realization and expanding market share.

He added that applying the technology strengthens existing solutions and builds precision-education capabilities that deliver content matched to the right moment across more than 100 million active curriculum licenses.
Eight AI learning tools are now live, with active users topping 7.5 million. Three more are coming this fiscal year. The company is also piloting AI projects outside education.

The standout is AI Reader, a tool that lets students highlight passages and quiz themselves inside e-books. Since its launch in fall 2024, it has logged 63 million learning interactions from about 2.6 million students through July 2026.

The business mix has also shifted. McGraw Hill said 64% of first-quarter revenue came from digital. Last year, print — hardcover and paperback combined — accounted for 73.1% of trade publishing revenue.
The Nerdy Novelist opened up Story Hacker OS for the first time in a 12-minute video. The title is itself a question: can AI really make a better novelist?

Story Hacker OS is a writing environment built on genre templates, story tropes and a book builder that assembles a full book. It places AI not where sentences get written for you, but where a story gets structured more solidly, leaving creative control in the writer's hands.
The video shows an actual project in progress. It opens a crime-thriller research bundle and several AI-generated story pitches to show exactly how far the tool gets involved.

He lays out five uses: targeting precisely what readers of your genre want, mining a pile of AI-generated pitches for usable seeds, learning craft itself, confidently entering a genre you haven't written in, and catching structural mistakes before a story falls apart.
Models connect directly through OpenRouter. The writer also sets the dial on how much AI to use. The video is brief but firm on this point: the story is still yours.

The Story Hacker community is offering a 7-day free trial. Amid a crowd of tools that generate whole prose, this one bets on propping up structure and tropes from below while leaving the final judgment to a human.

Crossref's new position paper makes a simple but important point: persistent identifiers, or PIDs, are a means, not an end. Their value doesn't come from the identifier string itself, but from the metadata, relationships, services and stewardship built around it. AI makes that distinction far more urgent.

blocks.cap: A river splitting into many branches

blocks.x: Research is no longer found only on journal pages and in indexes. The same paper can sit simultaneously on preprint servers, publisher platforms, institutional repositories, scholarly indexes and licensed AI collections. AI can pull a paragraph from any one of them, break it apart, and reuse the claim without passing through the context of the original page. Version ambiguity has become a provenance problem, not just a discovery problem.

Three common scenarios make the point. Preprints get revised multiple times before journal publication. Even after a final version is corrected or retracted, repository copies and downstream indexes can keep holding the old text. In post-publication peer review, a paper can pass through — or never reach — several review and revision states before, or without, arriving at a final version.

PIDs get attached in different ways. Some keep a single DOI even as the paper changes; others issue a new one for each version. Both approaches have their uses, but the identifier itself doesn't say what changed or which version is current. Even while a cited DOI resolves cleanly to the record being maintained, AI may still be reading an outdated copy.

The revised NISO Journal Article Versions recommendation has entered its final editing stage. It will soon go to NISO's voting members, and if approved, official release is expected this fall. The revision draws a clearer line between an article's stage and its status, then layers semantic versioning on top — a mechanism meant to distinguish even multiple changes made within the same stage.

blocks.cap: Three layers of version-aware AI access

blocks.x: Splitting the question into three makes it easier to sort out. What piece of research is this? PIDs like DOIs and their attached metadata answer that. What state is it in? Article stage, status and semantic version answer that. What did AI actually use? That's where provenance information comes in.

Someone reading an AI-generated literature review, policy summary or news article may never see the original page. A citation with only a DOI, even if accurate, isn't enough to retrace the evidentiary path. Version information isn't screen decoration — it becomes part of citation accuracy.

Until now, version information has been treated mainly as something to display — fine as long as it appeared on a landing page, a PDF, or a publication history field. In AI workflows, that information needs to intervene at the harvesting and retrieval stage. A retrieval system needs to know whether what it grabbed is a preprint, an accepted manuscript or a final version, and whether that version was later corrected, retracted or superseded.

When a final version is corrected on a publisher's page, that fact needs to flow through to repositories, indexes, licensed collections and AI services. Otherwise, AI keeps feeding on a version the scholarly community has already moved past. NISO's CREC recommendation has already mapped out how to create, transmit and display retraction, removal and expression-of-concern information.

The biggest risk sits with static collections. Once a collection is ingested, it hardens into that day's snapshot unless updates are pushed in. Mechanisms like STM's CUSAP notification protocol or GetFTR's retraction and correction service need to fill that gap. AI can already find a paper. The next step is making it disclose which version it read.

blocks.cap: The Creative Penn podcast, episode with Ricardo Fayet

blocks.x: Reedsy co-founder and CMO Ricardo Fayet sat down for more than an hour on The Creative Penn podcast. The question keeps coming back to one thing: when readers start asking AI for books instead of typing into a search box, how does my book end up inside that answer?

The AI recommendation process Fayet describes moves in three layers. It searches the web repeatedly to build a candidate list, ranks those candidates using review counts, ratings and mentions scattered across the internet, then runs a verification step to confirm the books actually fit before a title ever gets named.

blocks.cap: Reedsy co-founder and CMO Ricardo Fayet

blocks.x: Approaches built around keywords and search volume lose their grip here. A request like “an action-adventure thriller by a female indie author, with a female protagonist” has no search volume to speak of in the first place. Fayet calls this shift the move from SEO to GEO, or AIO.

Different AIs trust different sources. Claude leans heavily on Goodreads. ChatGPT and Gemini rely heavily on Reddit. Google has a paid partnership with Reddit, and Sam Altman holds a stake in Reddit. LinkedIn is useful for nonfiction, while BookTok still isn't well read by AI.

So what Fayet recommends is modest: Goodreads reviews, Listopia lists, book review sites, any page at all that carries the book's title. Build up a trail across the internet, he says. When there are multiple candidates, the book with more mentions is the one that survives into the recommendation.

Marketing still starts with finding comp titles. A concept nobody else has written is far more likely to die for lack of a market than to open a new one. The same conversation also produced the line that having a good book matters more than being a good marketer.

No matter how many platforms multiply, the one asset an author fully owns is an email list. Algorithms can't cut its reach, and the relationship built by replying directly to a reader's email doesn't come from social media.

Authors who last more than a decade share three things: a compulsion to write, a sense for weighing profit and loss, and resilience. Business sense is the judgment not to pour more ad money into a $3.99 book than the book itself earns; resilience is the strength to keep pushing a strategy for about six months even after the excitement from a conference has worn off.

Predictions that AI would erase jobs have missed so far. The U.S. unemployment rate hasn't shifted since ChatGPT's public release. Instead, the shape of work is changing. Translators sell AI-translation review. Editors polish AI-drafted manuscripts. Cover designers turn around concepts faster. Fayet's advice to authors is also hands-on rather than a course: pick one problem you've been putting off and throw it at AI. Paste Meta ad data into Claude and ask what else you'd need to know to understand this ad, and the conversation turns into analysis.

There was a short mention of Reedsy's own work too. Reedsy Studio, backed by 10 to 15 engineers, is adding plot maps, character relationship tracking, writing-goal statistics, free exports and Google Docs-style collaborative co-writing. So far, he says, there's no sign of AI eating into the marketplace.

Harriman House claims it is the first in commercial publishing to do this with the new book The Everything Code, by macro analyst and founder Raoul Pal. The book was made using an in-house AI tool trained only on Pal's own writing to date.

blocks.cap: Raoul Pal

blocks.x: The Bookseller reported the news in an article by Melina Spanoudi on August 20, 2026, using the phrase “AI-facilitated” book in the headline. Unlike handing a draft to some unspecified large language model, the publisher pinned down the training material as the work of a single author.
The rest of the article is behind registration and a paid subscription. A free account allows up to three articles a month, and subscriptions start at £3.65 a week.

In a short tip video called “The Automated Author” from Future Fiction Academy, Stacey Anderson shows writers a low-pressure way to step into coding interfaces like Codex and Claude Code. The starting point is that you don't need to become a programmer. No grand app, no big system, no building a whole piece of software is required.

All you need is a folder, a handful of markdown or text files, and an AI that can actually work inside those files. Anderson admits she herself put off switching because she already had skills and workflows running well in Claude Projects.

On screen, she poses the same question to both Codex and Claude Code: she's a self-publishing genre novelist who has been AI-writing through chat and project interfaces so far — is it worth switching? The answer became the video's title. A coding interface doesn't write prose any better. Claude in the chat window and Claude in the terminal are the same brain. What changes is the scope that brain can reach.

That's why file organization becomes the key. Anderson keeps one YAML file per book, holding the title, pen name, series, planned release date, and a status such as drafting, editing, draft, or published. The AI can scan the whole project without reading all 800 manuscripts. The difference grows as manuscripts, series bibles, style guides, marketing material, metadata, and publishing checklists pile up.

Start in a safe experimental folder — using copies, not the original manuscripts, in a space set aside just for AI, not your regular documents folder. Anderson made a separate R drive on her computer, for “robot,” and keeps all agent-related files there, broken down into books, series, manuscripts, outlines, editing, marketing, and publishing.

She writes rules into an agents.md or claude.md file. Her first rule is no deletion: moving things to an archive folder is fine, deleting them is not. She also flags the downsides. Reading files, thinking, and retrying burns more tokens, so a $20 plan hits its limit faster. The risk of overwriting is real too, so she backs up to the cloud several times a day and uses Git alongside it.

She ends with a demo. She asks the AI to write a short blog post about everything covered so far and drop it in the folder; a moment later, a markdown file appears in the experimental folder. Her closing point: once you've rewritten that post in your own voice, next time you don't need to spell out long rules — you can just say the older posts in this folder are my voice.

About two years ago, Maris Kreizman wrote about how pathetic the trend of chopping books into bullet points was. Her point was that we read and struggle with a text for reasons other than swallowing bite-sized pieces of knowledge.

Since then, as tech fascism has gained power, she sees both art and the experience of struggling in front of art as having lost their value entirely. Last week, Axios publisher Nicholas Johnson wrote a post about using AI as a “reading buddy” to work through themes and get help “understanding dense old prose.” To Kreizman, that amounted to bragging about outsourcing the very act of struggling while reading.

Her argument is that the more a world is captured by convenience, the more it should honor literary friction: writing that doesn't go down easy, that makes you sit with uncertainty or discomfort. That's where the path to growing as a reader and a thinker lies. She isn't knocking light, fast reading purely for pleasure. A book that goes down easy is fine too. It's just one kind of reading among many.

The kind of reading she means is what high schools and colleges used to teach. The nights in college when she pushed down the urge to go to the campus bar's “Thirsty Thursday” and instead worked her way through 880 pages of Middlemarch. All those nights at the bar blurred into one, but the memory of reading Middlemarch stayed.

Nor is this only about great works. Citing an article Megan Greenwell wrote for Wired, she notes that kids today can read the words just fine but can't make meaning out of them. One educator put it this way: “They're probably reading more than ever before. But it's all fragments.”

Criticism isn't safe either. As outlets fold up traditional book reviews in favor of more “user-friendly” formats, there's less room left for ambiguity. A good piece of book writing wrestles with a book rather than making lists out of it, she writes. She adds that most of the job postings coming her way on LinkedIn these days are asking her to let her editing career be used to train AI.

Reading Missouri Williams's new book The Vivisectors, she got lost, and she hates getting lost. Still, she underlined constantly. Once she stopped trying to decode it and let it flow like a poem, it finally became enjoyable. She sees an inability to sit with discomfort as feeding today's book bans and censorship. Thinking, learning, and growing don't fit a world leaning increasingly toward fascism, so she argues for pushing harder still. Questioning everything is how each of us can push back against that drift.

In a new survey from AI-detection company Originality.AI, 63% of religious paperbacks listed on Amazon were classified as likely written by AI. The analysis drew on 2,034 English-language paperbacks averaging four stars or higher across 14 faith- and belief-related categories.

Over the first half of 2026, the company scanned three elements of each book's public Amazon listing: the description, the author bio, and the book preview. Of these, the preview was the main yardstick. A score of 50 or above was grouped as “suspected AI.” The report's authors added that detection results only point to the likelihood of AI authorship, not proof of who wrote a given book.

Broken down by subgenre, Magic was highest at 78%, followed by Hinduism at 76% and Taoism at 74%. At the other end were Satanism at 22%, Atheism at 40%, and Mormonism at 42%. The report notes that the sample sizes for the latter three categories are smaller than for the first three, and offers one hypothesis for why Eastern religions ran especially high: “We believe non-native English speakers are using AI to enter the English-language market.”

Hinduism had the most books showing AI traces across all three elements—description, bio, and preview—at 72 books, or 25% of the Hinduism books sampled. Even counting books likely written by humans, the description was the element most likely to have been AI-generated.

An Amazon spokesperson pointed to the company's content guidelines, which don't prohibit AI-generated works: “We're working to build a store that readers love and that publishers and authors trust. We have numerous safeguards in place to protect that experience, and we continue to strengthen them. Our content guidelines determine what books can be sold, and we proactively prevent, detect, and remove content that violates them, whether it's AI-generated or not.”

Originality.AI has previously found that books likely written by AI are almost always cheaper and shorter than human-written ones. Religion was no different: suspected-AI books averaged $16.84 and 170 pages, while likely human-written books averaged $18.96 and 208 pages.

The report's authors view these books as a business built on exploiting faith: “Religious digital content has been fertile ground for AI slop since the earliest days of AI-generated memes. It touches the center of believers' faith, affirming what they already believe to be right, and in the case of books sold on Amazon, makes money doing it.”

U.S. textbook authors have filed another class action lawsuit against OpenAI, this time in New York. They allege that copyrighted textbooks were used without permission to train large language models, some of them downloaded from illegal pirate sites. Last July, the same authors filed a similar lawsuit against Meta in California.

blocks.cap: The lawsuit argues that if AI companies are allowed to keep “ingesting textbooks and continuously updating their contents with each new edition,” instructors and schools could abandon textbook adoption altogether in favor of LLM-based “substitutes.”

blocks.x: In the complaint filed on August 14, lead plaintiff Michael Sullivan and the other authors allege that OpenAI, backed by codefendant Microsoft, illegally copied thousands of textbooks to train its AI, stripped out copyright notices to “conceal” the conduct, and created a service that risks “displacing” the market for new textbooks and revised editions.

The complaint argues that a licensing market for using textbook content in training and paying “fair compensation” for it either already existed or could have been created, but that the defendants “circumvented” it. The authors reason that textbooks are “uniquely valuable for LLM training” because they treat “academic fields and subfields in an engaging, effective, and up-to-date” way.

What sets this case apart from other suits is market structure. General trade-book readers buy books “for personal reasons,” and readers seeking a specific author or specific book don't readily accept substitutes. Textbooks are different: “the end purchaser is not the person who chooses the book.” Instructors, schools, and education authorities decide through adoption and assign the book to students.

The complaint states: “Either way, the purchaser has a strong incentive not to pay for the textbook if they can find a 'free' version of the same book, or a 'good enough' substitute, from an LLM.” It also argues that while a textbook's “subject matter” may not be copyrightable, “the way the author selected, arranged, and ordered the material” and “the author's voice and manner of teaching” are protected.

The authors are seeking a ruling of copyright infringement, damages, and an injunction to prevent “further infringement.” According to ChatGPT is Eating the World, there are currently 136 lawsuits pending against AI companies.

Jon Bond appeared on the podcast run by Joanna Penn of The Creative Penn, where they talked about the difficulties of indie publishing and book marketing. Before co-founding Whitefox, he spent 35 years in traditional publishing, including stints at Penguin and HarperCollins, and he is also a co-author of “Going Indie: Publishing Your Book Your Way,” written with James Silver.

Bond believes that how much large publishers actually use AI, and the experimentation happening behind the scenes, go far beyond what's said publicly. “Whether the goal is boosting efficiency or just experimenting itself, there has to be a significant amount of work going on,” he says. Publishers often draw a line, saying “we use it only for marketing and operations, not for creative work or editing,” but he suspects there's considerable unreported use in areas like writing metadata, book descriptions, cover copy, and royalty calculations.

Whitefox, the company he's with, takes a different approach. “Going Indie” includes AI-generated chapter summaries as they are, and Bond explains that he included alongside them “ten commandments that I think are useful guidelines” for using AI responsibly. In other words, he chose disclosure over concealment.
He points out that publishers are “too cautious about saying what they do and don't do.” In other words, public statements alone make it hard to gauge how much AI the industry has actually adopted.

Frankfurt Rights, the rights-trading platform run by the Frankfurt Book Fair, explained why AI licensing requests still require case-by-case negotiation. Jenny Kühne, director of rights and licensing solutions at Frankfurter Buchmesse, says, “Individual AI deals are still too complex and varied to be handled through a standardized process.”

She names five variables. “The details vary considerably — from the intended use and scope of the license to compensation, reporting, and liability.” Because Frankfurt Rights isn't a collective licensing body, the actual contracts aren't automated, and rights holders and prospective users have to negotiate directly.

The platform is also dealing with another problem: attempts to scrape content without authorization. Kühne said, “Attacks on the website have increased noticeably, and we suspect it's AI bots looking for content.”

A response is already underway. “We already had security measures in place, but we strengthened them right away and keep monitoring,” she explains. She sees refining the legitimate-use process itself as a way to distinguish lawful access from unauthorized scraping.

The August 12 edition of Jane Friedman's weekly industry roundup, “Links of Interest,” covers three strands of AI news running across publishing. Alongside a piece on the publishing practice of not fact-checking memoirs, it places EU transparency rules, a journalism award, and remarks from HarperCollins's CEO side by side.
The first is the EU rules. It covers news that transparency rules requiring future models to embed watermarks and attach signed provenance metadata are on the way.

The second is a journalism award. It reports that entries self-disclosing AI use reached five this year, a record high. This reads as a sign that judging panels are becoming more willing to accept disclosed AI use.

The third is HarperCollins. It covers news that the major publisher's CEO called for an AI response that moves at the industry level, not just at individual companies. This points to where contract terms between authors and publishers may head next.

Dr. Alan Finkel, Australia's former chief scientist and founder of Proudly Human, issued a pointed warning about AI in an interview with The Bookseller. He states flatly that AI “provides no economic benefit whatsoever to the arts or creative industries.”
Finkel calls for stronger institutional safeguards to protect creators from AI-generated content. In his view, existing legal frameworks like copyright simply aren't enough.

What stands out is that someone who has worked on national science policy has stepped directly into a debate that had mostly been carried by authors' organizations and publishers. Proudly Human, the group he founded, speaks up for creators against the changes AI has brought to the arts.

In this episode of the ALLi Member Q&A podcast, hosts Michael La Ronn and Sacha Black discussed whether a $2,000 line edit could be replaced with AI, and where to draw the line between supplementing a human editor and replacing one.

blocks.cap: The ALLi Member Q&A podcast. Image source: ALLi Self-Publishing Advice Center

blocks.x: Listener Roco asked, “Is it acceptable and safe to use AI instead of spending $2,000 on a line edit?” Sacha Black said it's a question each person has to judge by their own morals, values, and ethics, so there's no black-and-white answer. She added that if you're wary of AI, there are several ways to get close to a copy-edit result without spending $2,000 — books on sentence craft, beta reading, authors reading for each other, or a one-month ProWritingAid subscription. Of course, ProWritingAid itself has AI built in, so avoiding it entirely is hard.

Michael La Ronn's answer was more blunt. He said AI can't replace an editor, and might never be able to. What he recommends isn't replacement but supplementation — using it to hand editors a cleaner manuscript, or as a last line of defense right before publication, after editing is done. He considers edit assistance at the level of catching typos to be among the more harmless uses of AI, but said it's a different matter once you move into having AI write the novel itself. Both hosts urged checking ALLi's AI policy first and disclosing AI use transparently.

A question about series covers also came up. Michael La Ronn said to keep color, typography, and overall structure consistent so readers recognize, within microseconds, “ah, that's book two of the XYZ series.” The worst case is handing book one and book two to different designers. Sacha Black said she's run into that on nearly all of her series, and in that case she gets written permission by email from the original designer to keep using the design. You have to check, item by item, whether the same information appears on the spine in the same orientation, down to matching font effects — because the design copyright belongs to the original designer.

For the IngramSpark returns question, Sacha Black answered by opening her dashboard directly. Last month she sold 1,316 copies with 22 returns, or 1.6%. Her conclusion: you just need to check once or twice a week that sales are outpacing returns.

The AI models that power ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude train on hundreds of millions of books, online articles, academic papers, and nearly everything else findable on the internet. Most established authors have, without knowing it and without ever consenting, helped build the very tool now threatening their livelihood. It looks illegal, but reality isn't that simple.

blocks.cap: Image source: NanoStockk / Getty Images

blocks.x: Cathy Gellis, an attorney who works across intellectual property, copyright, and technology, told TechCrunch, “Part of the problem is there's just so much happening across this whole area of law and this whole area of technology,” adding, “It's very complicated, and feelings are raw on both sides.”

Last year, Judge William Alsup ordered Anthropic to pay authors $1.5 billion. It looks like a win for authors on the surface, but Alsup ruled that Anthropic's AI training itself was lawful. What he took issue with was stealing books from illegal shadow libraries. The judge wrote that “Anthropic's LLMs trained upon works not to race ahead and replicate or supplant them — but to turn a hard corner and create something different,” much as an aspiring writer who is a reader might do. Gellis sees the ruling as more favorable to AI companies — what weight does a $1.5 billion fine carry for a company projected to post $200 billion in annual revenue by 2028?

Copyright law hasn't been touched since 1976. Judges now have to answer questions that will shape the future of the AI industry using 50-year-old guidance. Jason Henderson, founding and senior attorney of the IP and media practice at JWL International, said, “The law is all over the place, so everyone is quite worried right now,” adding, “We know AI models trained on all that material, but the law hasn't caught up to that question yet.”

The disputes mostly turn on fair use, and specifically on whether using the copyrighted work is sufficiently “transformative.” Henderson explained that “copyright has always been about protecting and growing markets” — if you use someone else's property for training with the direct intent to compete, courts tend to take a dim view, but there's room to find it acceptable if you don't compete. Thomson Reuters' lawsuit against Ross Intelligence, which copied Thomson Reuters' content to build a competing legal platform, is one such case. Judge Stephanos Bibas wrote that “Ross's use wasn't transformative, because it didn't have a further purpose or different character” from Thomson Reuters' own use. The argument that a chatbot competes with an author by generating new synthetic books from that author's writing hasn't held up in court yet.

Copyright over AI-generated output is a separate issue. In Thaler v. Perlmutter, the court found that work created 100% by AI cannot receive copyright protection. That opens a new headache: how do you prove whether a work was made by AI, and if so, what percentage of it? With most AI companies still tied up in litigation, a definitive answer won't arrive anytime soon.

Book Insights is a Gemini-powered reading assistant built into Google Play Books. It summarizes chapters, untangles confusing sentences, tracks characters, and answers spoiler-free questions about select English ebooks — all without leaving the page you're reading. It just launched worldwide in the Google Books and Audiobooks app for Android.

blocks.cap: Book Insights in Google Play Books. Image source: Good e-Reader

blocks.x: When you come back to a book you left off reading, you don't need to flip back through earlier chapters. Book Insights' “Catch me up” summarizes what you've read so far. On a book with Book Insights enabled, tap the lightbulb icon in the upper right, then tap the “Catch me up” button to get the summary.

Questions tend to come up as you read, and now you can look them up without closing the book. If you hit a puzzling passage while reading a Shakespeare play, you can highlight it and get a few questions that unpack its meaning. The follow-up suggested questions tie the clues in the book together more tightly.

If none of the suggested questions fit, you can type your own into the “Ask Play Books” box. In a novel with a large cast, you might ask something like “Has this character appeared before?” to retrace the context. Answers are designed to reference only the text up to where you currently are, to avoid spoilers. That said, generative AI is still experimental and isn't always accurate.

Book Insights currently works only with select English ebooks. You can check which books qualify via the “Tools” badge on the book's detail page. The badge shows which AI tools are available, including Book Insights. To use it, open the book and tap the lightbulb icon at the top of the Android Play Books app or the web reader, or just highlight any sentence.
Spotify has rolled out three new audiobook features in quick succession over the past few months.

Whether it's an epic fantasy or a celebrity memoir, time spent lost in a good book is never wasted. Spotify is trying to push that experience further with three features: one that builds playlists matched to your taste, one that lets you explore your interests through conversation, and one that lets you keep going on a series you love.

James Jacoby, Senior Director of Engineering & Insights for audiobooks, said, “Books have become one of the ways users connect most deeply with Spotify,” and that “these features are focused on lowering the barrier between listeners and books they'll love.”

First, “Prompted Playlists” lets you simply describe, in words, the kind of book you want, and it builds a custom playlist that reflects your taste and current literary trends. For example, you could ask for “a list of books adapted into film or TV in the last three years that got praise from critics or audiences,” or “build me an audiobook calendar, one book a month starting this month, each under 15 hours, matched to that month's mood and my taste.” It's currently in beta for some Premium users in the US, Canada, the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, and Sweden.

The second feature, “Just Ask Spotify,” lets you talk directly to Spotify by text or voice. Ask something like “recommend some Scandinavian noir to read before my trip to Sweden,” and it will answer follow-up questions too, moving fluidly across music, podcasts, and audiobooks. It's currently offered in English to Premium users 18 and older in the US, Ireland, and Sweden.

Third, once you finish one book in a series, Spotify immediately recommends the next installment, and multi-book series are now tagged so you don't lose track of the order. You can also see all of an author's series at a glance on their author profile page. This feature is available in the US, Canada, the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, and Sweden.

blocks.cap: A Spotify app screen showing Rebecca Yarros' “Fourth Wing” series and an audiobook playlist.

blocks.x: It's well known that Games Workshop takes a hard line on AI. Even so, an IGN reporter was surprised to hear a narrator read, out loud, a warning against training AI on the novel in one of their current favorite Warhammer 40,000 audiobooks.

blocks.cap: Image source: Games Workshop

blocks.x: Training AI on books without permission is already a major topic in the industry. Last week, 404 Media reported that Amazon had been “buying up enormous quantities of books, scanning them for AI training data, and discarding them in the process.” Last summer, it came out that Anthropic had shredded millions of physical books to train Claude. That secret project, called 'Project Panama,' surfaced through a lawsuit filed by authors, and Anthropic settled for $1.5 billion even after largely winning on the fair use question.

AI warnings are posted all over the Games Workshop site. The Black Library website, which handles the book business, states that it “expressly prohibits the use of website content to train generative artificial intelligence (AI) technology.” The legal notices section also carries a detailed AI warning.

This time, at the end of the audiobook for The Wicked and The Warped, a Necron novel by Robert Rath, narrator Richard Reed read the following: “This recording is copyright Games Workshop 2026. All rights reserved. It may not be used or reproduced in any way for text and data mining activities, or for the development or training of artificial intelligence models or systems.” It was the first time the reporter had heard a Black Library narrator read an AI warning out loud. There's no such warning at the end of Dan Abnett's Hive audiobook, released in May.

blocks.cap: The Wicked and the Warped. Image source: Games Workshop

blocks.x: Games Workshop banned AI use in content creation and design in January, and in July reaffirmed its anti-AI stance while saying it had investigated a marketing mistake that raised AI suspicions. CEO Kevin Rountree said, “We don't use AI at Games Workshop for product design or IP creation, and this will protect the integrity and ownership of our IP.”

The question is how effective this actually is. The tech industry invokes fair use to scrape creative works, including books, and that logic is still holding up even as major lawsuits and investigative reporting pile up. In March 2025, The Atlantic reported that Meta had pirated millions of books to train AI, and novels by Black Library authors were also found inside LibGen, the pirated-book database Meta used. Rountree recently acknowledged that AI now comes bundled automatically into third-party software “whether we like it or not,” adding that it's “just something we have to live with and keep an eye on.”
This is the August 13, 2026 edition of ALLi's Self-Publishing News, hosted by Dale L. Roberts. The headline makes the point plainly: Europe's new AI rules are reaching writers worldwide.

According to the video description, AI transparency is becoming a thornier issue for writers. The European Commission's 「Guidelines on transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems」 comes up at the 4:09 mark, followed by how Claude labels AI-generated content starting at 4:38. The point is that a rule made in Europe is starting to affect Claude users outside Europe too.
Starting at 6:34, the other side of the story comes in. Citing Sean Goedecke's piece 「Text AI watermarks are always easy to remove」, it points out how technically flimsy the labeling requirement is.

At 8:01, a study reported by the BBC comes up, finding that people preferred AI-written stories over human-written ones. At 9:06, a Nieman Lab article follows, noting that eight Pulitzer winners disclosed using AI this year, the most ever.

The rest covers industry numbers and practical matters: $33.4 billion in 2025 publishing revenue tallied by Publishers Weekly, an author who sold 1,000 copies of a self-published memoir in five months, Instagram's new book feature, and tightening YouTube Partner Program monetization requirements starting in 2027, one after another.

blocks.cap: An op-ed by Nigel George — Creation and publishing in the age of AI

blocks.x: This is an op-ed by Nigel George, an indie author, ALLi member, and founder of GNW Independent Publishing. The opening line is: “'No' is a complete sentence in itself.”

These are frightening times for writers. Algorithms demand endless output, and as AI slop spreads, the social media reach that was already narrow has shrunk further. The big AI companies say their AI is the next stage of human evolution and that you cannot survive without getting on board. To George, that looks more like a race to the bottom.
He says he has both a technical brain and a creative brain. The technical brain knows one fact: for AI to advance further, it needs us.

He suggests recalling the words commonly used about AI: it hallucinates, lies, thinks, understands, learns, remembers, wants, decides, creates. What actually happens inside the box is, in order, sampling error and statistical mispredictions, probability and weight calculations, context caching and RAG, function minimization and algorithm execution, interpolation and diffusion. The moment we lend human qualities to a machine, we cheapen the real human intelligence that built it.

He points out that when John McCarthy coined the term 'Artificial Intelligence' in 1955, it was branding, not a scientific proposition. Real intelligence requires lived experience, a sense of time, an understanding of causation, and intent. AI can imitate Shakespeare, but it cannot become Shakespeare.

George names three pillars of creative agency. First, know your own 'no.' His line is clear: AI does not get on the page in creative writing. He works full time coaching other writers, writing fiction and nonfiction, and publishing his own work, and he admits he couldn't produce even half that output without the AI tools he's built himself. Still, he doesn't touch the creative output itself.

Second, copyright belongs to humans. As AI slop floods the internet, frontier models risk a decline in output quality if they can't keep getting clean human data. That, he believes, is why the tech industry keeps trying to water down copyright law. The response is to make and enforce laws that keep copyright off AI-generated works, and to support labeling content as 'human-made.'

Third, it's just a machine. However uncanny the output, AI is an extremely sophisticated statistical calculator. It has no moral sense, no intuition, no experience, no understanding. Whatever ability it appears to show is simply a reflection of the humans who built it. George says this is a chance for writers to prove AI can grow human creativity rather than replace it, and returns to his opening line: “'No' is a complete sentence in itself.”

blocks.cap: The Publishing Technology Radar survey closes on August 30

blocks.x: The Digital Publishing Report has teamed up with Publishing Signal, an international initiative by knk, to create The Publishing Technology Radar. The first report comes out later this year.

Published once a year, the report splits technologies into four stages: watch, explore, pilot, and grow in earnest. The idea is for publishers to gauge where to invest, where to wait, and where they risk falling behind if they do nothing.

blocks.cap: Ingenta Aperture — a self-service portal that opens up rights and royalty data

blocks.x: Royalty statements vary in format from one publisher to another. They're hard to decode and usually come out only two or three times a year. On the side processing hundreds or thousands at once, small errors that any writer would spot instantly go unnoticed.

So most writers don't dig further if the royalty amount looks roughly right. Even a writer determined to check line by line is working with reporting cycles so infrequent that months or years can pass before a problem surfaces. By then, gathering the evidence to back up a claim isn't easy.

Publishing systems and workflows keep improving through technology, but royalties alone remain opaque. It's a point of friction that has long existed between publishers and creators. Even when a report is accurate, the absence of real-time information breeds needless suspicion and tension.

Erin L. Cox writes that fixing the systems handling contracts, rights, and royalties matters more outside the publishing house than inside it, when dealing with writers, license holders, agents, and publishing partners. What's at stake isn't just the immediate rights sale, but the trust that leads to the next deal.

Ingenta, founded in 1977, has built rights management tools with publishing partners, and the result is Ingenta Aperture. It's a self-service portal that opens up rights and royalty data securely, the moment it's requested. It runs on web, tablet, and mobile, is configured to a publisher's workflow, and connects to existing in-house systems. Information publishers choose to show, like sales by format, royalties by region, and payment history, updates the instant the in-house system updates, so writers never have to wait for a lag.

Over the past two years, publishers have been trying new and complex deals on writers' behalf, like LLM training licenses, microdeals, and multi-region, multi-format rights. The more such opportunities open up, the more rights holders need to trust their publisher. A publisher that hasn't built up trust misses time-limited deals and loses its edge in the market. Writers expect publishers to lead the way through the unfamiliar world of AI licensing, and the more information they get, the more willing they are to take part.

Rights holders now expect the same visibility into their own income that they get from online banking or asset management apps. Fully opening up rights income ultimately means addressing the human side of rights and royalty management, Cox concludes. This article was sponsored by Ingenta.

blocks.cap: Carlo Carrenho's Monday roundup of international publishing news

blocks.x: According to Börsenblatt, German children's book publisher Carlsen, along with author Marc-Uwe Kling and illustrator Astrid Henn, has filed suit against OpenAI. They allege infringement of the rights attached to the bestselling picture book 'Das NEINHORN.'

Carlsen views these outputs as evidence that the original NEINHORN material was used without permission to train language and image models.

The same briefing also covered a case of AI entering the publishing business. Publitik, reported by Brazil's PublishNews, is a subscription-based market intelligence platform that scans news, research, bestseller lists, and social media trends across the global book industry in real time. AI agents gather information from trade and general media in dozens of countries, and publishing professionals set up their own custom alerts by topic, market, author, or book.

Subscribers currently number around 100, and a mobile app is targeted for launch within the year. It's offered in both English and Portuguese, and aims to gather bestseller lists from multiple countries in one place. It's an attempt to get a broad view of what's selling in which markets and which books are emerging as global bestsellers.

blocks.cap: ALLi Self-Publishing News podcast — hosted by Dan Holloway

blocks.x: This week's Self-Publishing News podcast, hosted by ALLi news editor Dan Holloway, carries two welcome pieces of news for indie authors and one study worth chewing over.

The first is the launch of the Indie Manga Alliance. This newly formed US organization represents manga creators and publishers who sit outside the mainstream and outside the big publishers. It started with five independent publishers but envisions a much broader organization. Right now it is running a survey asking what people want from a group that represents the interests of indie manga creators and publishers, and it explicitly states that responses from writers and illustrators are welcome.

Manga has been growing in popularity outside Japan for quite some time. As online platforms like webtoons have grown, publishing graphic novels digitally has become easier, and indie creators have been doing the same in print. This launch effectively gives that trend an organization.

The second is Libro.fm. The audiobook platform Libro.fm, like Bookshop.org, is designed so that no matter where in the world a reader buys from, part of the price goes to a local bookstore the reader chooses. When someone buys an audiobook on Bookshop.org, the order passes to Libro.fm. This news is different: Libro.fm is moving into e-books.

The subscription model stays the same. Libro subscribers can spend their credits across e-books and audiobooks interchangeably, and part of the price still goes to a local bookstore. For now it is open in beta to indie bookstores first. Once bookstores receive advance e-book galleys and work out what they need, it will open to general readers in 2027. What becomes of the partnership with Bookshop is not yet clear.

The third item is the study in question: Bot or Not? Can People Tell the Difference Between Stories Written by a Human or by an AI System?, published by Cambridge University Press and written by Sydney Sears and Deena Skolnick Weisberg. The answer, as you'd guess, is no.

The first study involved 1,682 participants. Each read one story at a time, drawn from a mix of AI-written and human-written pieces, and was told the author was either ChatGPT or a human. They were then asked whether the story was high quality and whether it was engaging. On both measures, the highest-scoring story was one labeled as human-written but actually written by AI. Being labeled human carries value — but that value didn't necessarily follow the actual writing.

In the second batch, participants weren't told who the author was and had to guess whether a human or an AI had written it. People couldn't tell the difference. The interesting part was self-assessment: those who called themselves tech experts did better than random chance, but those who called themselves literature experts did no better than pinning the tail on the donkey.

Holloway's closing is brief: the days of saying AI could never produce writing people would want to read are already behind us. In the authors' own words, a serious conversation is needed about what creativity actually is.

blocks.cap: Book Riot's library news roundup, August 2026

blocks.x: This is Book Riot's August roundup of library news. This edition covers the AI upheaval that hit the Heated Rivalry fanfic community, “weird girl lit,” and the fuss around the upcoming Children of Blood and Bone.

Start with the AI items. More artists are lawyering up against AI. The roundup also traces how AI-made books are seeping onto bookstore shelves. The uproar when AI showed up in the Heated Rivalry fanfic community was something else entirely. The question of why Anthropic is destroying books also made the list, and HarperCollins CEO Brian Murray spoke up about the AI authorship problem.
The piece is paywalled, but the gist is clear: in a new study, readers gave AI-generated stories they believed were human-written higher scores than actual human-written stories.
Maybe that's why more writers are deliberately changing their style, even leaving in typos on purpose, as a defense against being mistaken for AI.

Boomers haven't stopped gifting their grandchildren shoddy AI-churned books, either. The writer notes this feels like the kind of thing library staff will start fielding questions about, adding that it brings to mind the mass-produced, name-personalized books of the '90s.

The rest of the roundup covers readers' advisory material, audiobooks, and screen adaptation news. Podium Entertainment, teaming up with the podcast network Realm, is turning 35 serialized fiction podcasts into audiobooks, and John Green revealed the audiobook casting for his new book, Hollywood, Ending. Apple TV picked up the rights to Rebecca Yarros's new romance, Peculiar Stars.
The author, Frances Pinter, is the founder of SUPRR, which supports the recovery and rebuilding of Ukrainian publishing.

The academic publishing ecosystem is badly shaken. The crisis in university monographs isn't a hypothesis, it's a number on the balance sheet. In the West, print sales of humanities and social science scholarly books have fallen 40 to 50 percent over the past decade, and the financial runway for open-access (OA) models is precarious. On top of that comes the pressure from artificial intelligence.

blocks.cap: Books stacked on shelves — a Scholarly Kitchen guest post on the monograph crisis

blocks.x: On May 29, 2026, a LabHub discussion titled “From Shelves and Drawers to Millions of Readers” was held at the International Book Arsenal Festival in Kyiv. It was organized by the NRFU project ecosystem and Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv (TSNUK), with support from SUPRR. The event quickly turned into a debate over the economics of knowledge, rights management, and new business structures.

Pinter put her finger on the sorest spot first. The classic Book Processing Charge (BPC) model, in which an author or their institution pays $8,000 to $15,000 upfront, simply doesn't work for Eastern European institutions. Diamond OA, or library-funded consortia such as Opening the Future, COPIM, and Subscribe-to-Open, also depend on having a stable funding source to run.

Victor Kruhlov, head of Ranok publishing house, had a cold-eyed answer. No country in the world still has retail demand left for specialized academic monographs. According to Book Chamber data, the average print run for academic monographs from 2022 to 2025 was 100 to 300 copies. An upfront grant of around $3,000 to $5,000 per book covers blind peer review, copyediting, metadata indexing, and DOI assignment. Print is minimized through print-on-demand, and the digital edition is released as Diamond OA. What a foundation is buying isn't paper, but verified quality and discoverability.

Hanna Kharlamova leans toward a hybrid institutional model. Individual BPCs are close to fantasy given today's economic conditions. The idea is to bind major higher-education institutions, like the more than ten universities gathered at LabHub, into a single open-access publishing network, pooling the publishing budgets each university used to run separately to support one national-level open-science platform.

In 2026, artificial intelligence became the first consumer to read and filter academic research. Valentyn Sobchuk raised the sharpest point. Thousands of Ukrainian research papers are locked away in university repositories as low-resolution, unsearchable PDFs. Worse, they effectively don't exist to AI crawlers. Only with clean metadata, machine-readable structure, and explicit Creative Commons licenses will Ukrainian scholarship's voice make it into the answers given by tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Consensus, or Elicit.

Olha Poliukhovych proposed counting public lectures and popular-science writing toward faculty evaluation, while Hanna Tolstanova insisted blind peer review is a line that must not be crossed. Yana Sychikova pointed to rights management as the weakest link. It's common for a professor to sign away all subsidiary rights in a contract with a foreign publisher, so that the university loses even the right to post the book in its own repository.

Kharlamova's message to the global publishing world fits in one sentence: this isn't a request for charity, but a proposal for an equal intellectual partnership. Ukraine has accumulated raw material that the global academic community needs, from macroeconomic resilience to cognitive security and cyber defense. What it needs in return is publishing infrastructure, rights-management training, and distribution networks.

blocks.cap: A robot reading a book — Photo Andrea De Santis, Unsplash

blocks.x: Book Riot's newsletter has gathered recent AI news from the publishing world in one place. AI-generated text has already made its way into mainstream publishing, and the discussion over where and how to deal with that reality is turning a corner.
First, the uncanny valley. David Corn of Mother Jones wrote a novel using Claude, whose protagonist is a writer who writes a novel using Claude. After a few retries, the result was “not that bad.”

The title is The Ghost in the Machine, chosen by Claude. Flaws and all, Corn read it to the end. “I wanted to keep reading. The plot was tight, and even knowing what was coming, the journey toward the narrative milestones I'd requested made for a good drive. There were surprising moments along the way, too.”

The EU shows up here too. The same body that made Apple give up the Lightning port has now told AI companies to “add machine-readable markers so that AI-generated or manipulated content can be detected.” The first to answer publicly was Anthropic, which announced last week that it will watermark text generated and edited by its large language models (LLMs), including Claude.

Who detects the detector? New York Times tech reporter Brian X. Chen ran the AI detection program Pangram dozens of times and summed it up this way: “This ability to catch bot-made words will be very useful for filtering out annoyances” — things like scam emails, LinkedIn filler, and fake reviews. Substack has also bet heavily on Pangram, adding a new tool that lets creators and readers scan writing on the platform themselves.

Some favor prevention over cure. Writer Vera Kurian built AuthorProof, an app that helps writers prove their manuscript wasn't written by AI. Rather than detection software, it captures the writing process itself, built tight enough that faking it would be brutally tedious.
The newsletter closes with a reader survey, asking people to draw their own line on what counts as AI-written text.

blocks.cap: The Bookseller

blocks.x: David James wrote for The Bookseller, arguing that submission guidelines banning any use of AI are unfairly shutting out disabled writers.
The real issue isn't misuse but accessibility. Writers who use the technology responsibly get caught in the same one-line ban.

blocks.cap: Authors who never existed

blocks.x: “Elena Vasquez and Marcus Chen have appeared as volcanologists, as astronauts, as thriller protagonists, as podcast hosts, and as co-authors on academic papers in hundreds of AI-generated documents, despite never having lived.” That's a line from a new preprint by researchers at Samsung and the University of Warsaw.

The paper compiled names that have appeared as co-authors on hundreds of AI-generated papers, articles, and books. These are people who don't exist, names that large language models keep producing over and over when asked to invent an expert in a given field.

The paper is titled 「The Ghost Couple: Correlated LLM Name Priors and Their Haunting of the Web and Academic Publishing」. Last June, 404 Media reported that ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude favor the name Elias Sohn when writing fiction, and that the character is usually a lighthouse keeper. There was also an observation that ChatGPT produces Marcus Chen when asked to invent a software developer.

blocks.cap: From the paper 「The Ghost Couple」

blocks.x: What the researchers showed goes beyond overlapping names. The models produce “correlated character ensembles” — meaning certain names have a high probability of appearing together. Claude's Elena Amara Okafor, Gemini's Aris Sohn and Lena Petrova, and ChatGPT's Elara Voss also came up repeatedly.

Earlier this month, 404 Media covered Research Gold. It presented itself as human-conducted medical research, but all of it was AI-generated, and the name of its founder and chief methodologist was Elena Vasquez. After the report, the company removed the name from its site. In the Facebook rumors that spread after Alex Pretti died at the hands of U.S. Border Patrol agents in January, Snopes reported that the false claims were also attributed to a nonexistent “Director Elena Vasquez.”

First author Michał Brzozowski also dug through academic databases. “On Zenodo, which is run by CERN and issues real DataCite DOIs, we confirmed 1,655 ghost-author records that invented nonexistent journals and faked publication dates.” Anyone with a free account can mint a DOI, but the problem is that the DOI then spreads outward. “It's a real DOI that any academic harvester can scrape. The groundwork for contaminating the academic record at scale is already in place. (…) The academic record is quietly being haunted.” Ghost names form synthetic research groups on ResearchGate and get indexed without verification on Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar.

The researchers believe that because the names appear so consistently across models and versions, they can be used to trace the origin of AI slop. Elena Vasquez showed up especially often in text generated by Claude Sonnet 4. Brzozowski noted, though, that this accuracy may not last, since AI-generated material carrying these names is flooding the internet and getting pulled back into training data.

The story of AI shaking up academic publishing isn't new. There have been earlier reports of scientific journals publishing AI-written sentences, of effects on peer review, and of the preprint repository arXiv deciding to ban authors of AI-generated submissions for a year. What's useful about this study is that these names offer a clue for spotting AI-generated material more easily.

blocks.cap: Entrance to the Amazon VGT3 facility

blocks.x: Last week, 404 Media reported on a warehouse where Amazon scans and then discards thousands of books to obtain AI training data. Below is an interview with an Amazon employee who worked at that warehouse. The employee isn't authorized to speak to the press, so they're identified anonymously. Edited for length and clarity.

This employee worked at Amazon's VGT3 warehouse. It shares a building with LAS8, which runs a print-on-demand business, and both belong to Amazon's facility complex in Las Vegas, Nevada. 404 Media placed a tracker in a shipment of rare books from a used bookstore that it suspected was being bought up by an anonymous AI company, and the shipment traveled across the U.S. to reach VGT3.
— What do you do when you clock in at VGT3?

“You have to walk all the way to the back of the warehouse. That's where I first saw the scanners and wondered what on earth they were for. When I asked someone, they said even the people working there didn't seem to know what they were doing. Once I got closer and pieced things together, I roughly figured it out. I also saw them cutting the spines off books. Once scanning is done, the loose pages get thrown into a big shuttle bin. Everything gets mixed together, so there's no way to put a book back together.”
— What kinds of books are these?

“All kinds of books come in. At first there were a lot of new books, and some used ones too. Some clearly looked like library discards. We also got boxes from London, a lot of them University of London books. There were documents bound with staples, too — they said they'd been submitted to Parliament on Her Majesty's behalf. I saw a lot of German and Russian books, and Japanese books came in by the pallet. There were sealed new books as well.”

“Our job was to unpack the boxes. Honestly, that side of things looked like a mess. There was no real management or organization, and the process changed every day. We put books into totes and passed them on to scanning and sorting, and then other people cut off the bindings. One day, our job was to throw duplicates and books marked ‘we don't need this’ into a different shuttle bin. They weren't placed gently — just tossed in. They say the books get returned to vendors, but when they're piled up six or seven feet high in a shuttle bin like that, I wonder if the vendor really assesses each one's value.”
— What's it like watching the spine-cutting?

“It's a machine operated by a person. It looks like a small workstation, with one person assigned per machine. There's a cover and a separate slot for pushing the book in, so it's pretty safe. You pull your hand out, press a button, and a blade comes down and cuts it. There are at least twenty scanners, maybe as many as twenty-five. They look like bill-counting machines and flip through pages very fast. You can see a screen where the scanned pages fly by at an incredible speed.”
— What do you think about Amazon doing this?

“At first they said it was for Kindle, and I didn't believe it. I figured there was no way, given publishing rights and copyright issues. Then I learned it was for AI. What I don't like is that I can't take these books home myself. There's an enormous amount of knowledge inside them, and some of them look like rare books. I even heard that they actually order rare books. What bothers me is that they can't even be reused afterward — that means fewer books that other people get to see.”
Google has launched “Expert Intelligence.” It's a feature that lets readers pull from e-books they've already purchased and from verified sources directly within Google's AI products.

blocks.cap: Photo: Shutterstock

blocks.x: The initial lineup already covers more than 100,000 publisher titles. This is the first time a path for a book to become, through a formal license, material for an AI's answer has been laid out at this scale.

The story was written by Melina Spanoudi of The Bookseller on September 1. The article's body is behind a subscription wall, so what's confirmed from what's publicly available only goes as far as the announcement's outline.
Even so, the shape of it is clear. In the spot once held by a link to search results now sits a licensed answer.
For publishers, this is an issue that moves contracts and distribution strategy all at once. Where to draw the line in rights negotiations has become a point of contention again.

Starting August 2, Anthropic adds an invisible watermark to every piece of text and file Claude produces. The move is meant to comply with the EU AI Act's transparency provisions, but it applies worldwide, not just in Europe. The method follows SynthID Text, which Google DeepMind released in 2024.

The controversy starts with where the mark lands. Even when Claude is only asked to edit — proofreading, translating, or summarizing — rather than write something new, the output still carries the watermark. Anthropic itself has stressed that the mark is only a signal, not evidence. Detecting it only tells you the text passed through Claude at some point; it doesn't say who wrote it.

Article 50 of the EU AI Act actually states that this obligation does not apply when AI merely assists with standard editing or doesn't substantially alter the input. Watermarking editing assistance as well goes beyond what the law requires — and that's where the compliance theater critique comes in.

The provision itself carries real weight. Article 50's transparency obligation took effect on August 2. Violations carry a fine of up to €15 million or 3% of global annual revenue, whichever is greater.

There's a gap in the opposite direction too. If a sentence is heavily rewritten, translated into another language, or very short, even genuine Claude-written text won't register a mark. The same goes for output from older models that never watermarked at all.
This article by Jane Friedman is available in full only to paid subscribers.

blocks.cap: The Scholarly Kitchen

blocks.x: Almost nothing is certain about the value and future of AI in scholarly communication. David Crotty writes that there is exactly one certainty: people who hate AI really hate it, and they want to make sure you know it. The Scholarly Kitchen (TSK) has spent recent months learning about AI, and it has laid out what it's learned along with its current policy.

A few months ago, there was a guest post that ran an AI-generated image sent in by a contributor, unchanged. The reaction was fast and largely heated. No one seemed interested in the content of the piece itself. All anyone talked about was the “slop” image — which wasn't especially excessive or wrong. Had it not been labeled as AI-generated, most people probably would have scrolled right past it. In the end, it was swapped for a much more boring human-made image.

After that, reader emails started coming in. At first it was about once a month; now it's several a day. They say a TSK piece “seems” to have been written by AI, or that running some AI detector somewhere produced a result saying AI wrote it.

One such complaint became the occasion for TSK to put together a piece with Nature News. Reporter Richard Van Noorden dug in and found that tools like Pangram and GPTZero have sharply improved their accuracy, but plenty of low-quality tools are still on the market. More importantly, even the best tools can't tell AI-generated writing apart from AI-polished writing. Text written by AI from scratch, text written entirely by a human and only translated into English by AI, and text where only the proofreading was handed to AI all get slapped with the same “AI-generated” label.

Nature News put it this way: “No matter how good AI detection gets, there's a limit it can't escape. Researchers say the software can flag where AI was involved in a piece of writing, but it can't prove how it was used or judge whether that use is ethically acceptable.”
One TSK writer ran their own report through Pangram. It got the number right — 9% AI-generated — but it misidentified which parts were AI and which were human.

TSK's policy is this: AI tools can't be listed as authors. AI-generated images don't get published unless there's a specific reason to. That said, writers, editors, and reviewers are allowed to use AI for drafting and editing, as long as they transparently record that they used it. Disclosure has been left to writers' discretion, but as Avi Staiman has pointed out in two recent pieces, writers are reluctant to make that kind of declaration. His point was that banning the tools outright just means people use them anyway and lie about it. So now TSK asks for disclosure directly.

There's also a new bias created by the AI backlash. Instead of actually evaluating an argument you don't like, declaring it “AI” lets you skip the thinking altogether. Papers with awkward spelling and grammar getting pushed aside in review regardless of the quality of the research is an old problem, and there was hope that AI would strip that bias away for non-native English researchers. Instead, a climate of rejecting anything AI has touched has created one more bias.

Crotty himself doesn't use AI tools at all. To him, writing is thinking. Outsourcing the writing, he said, amounts to outsourcing the thinking. What worries him is the rise of writing that's ordinary and all looks alike. Large language models are machines that predict the next word, so they pull everything toward the middle. As with research, value in writing sits at the extremes, and if everything gets pulled into the middle of a bell curve, all that's left is homogenization and missed discoveries.
